0a.text: Question eighteen. Set up a double integral for the average value of f of x, y, equals eight minus four x squared, over the triangle D, with corners at zero zero, zero five, and five five.

0b.text: Here is the answer that got marked wrong. And here is the answer key.

0c.text: Let's work out exactly what went wrong, and, just as important, what didn't.

1a.text: First, what you actually submitted. One over thirteen point five, times the integral from zero to five, of the integral from zero to y, of eight minus four x squared, d x, d y.

1b.text: Look at the bounds. The inner integral says x runs from zero up to y. That's a horizontal strip.

1c.text: The outer integral says y runs from zero up to five. So the strip sweeps upward, and paints in a region.

1d.text: Put together, the bounds say: zero, is at most x, is at most y, is at most five. That is precisely the triangle with corners zero zero, zero five, and five five.

1e.text: The answer key just integrates in the other order. y goes first, from x up to five. Then x, from zero to five.

1f.text: Those are vertical strips, sweeping left to right. Same inequalities. Same triangle.

1g.text: Both orders cover the same region. The order of integration was not a mathematical error.

2a.text: So what was wrong? The number out front.

2b.text: The triangle has base five and height five. So its area is one half, times five, times five. That's twenty-five halves, or twelve point five.

2c.text: An average divides by that area. And one over twelve point five is two over twenty-five. Not one over thirteen point five.

2d.text: So, keeping your exact order of integration, a correct answer is two over twenty-five, times the very same double integral.

2e.text: You had the average value structure, the function, and the region right. The denominator was the one remaining error. That is the strongest argument to bring to your professor.

3a.text: Now the conceptual knot. What is the triangle, and what is the height?

3b.text: You're right that the output can be read as a height: z equals f of x, y, which is eight minus four x squared.

3c.text: The distinction is this. The triangle specifies the input locations, the points x, y, down on the floor. The function assigns a height, z, to each of those locations.

3d.text: For example, the point two, three lies inside the triangle, because zero is less than two, is less than three, is less than five.

3e.text: At that location, f of two, three is eight minus four times two squared, which is negative eight.

3f.text: So the matching point on the surface is two, three, negative eight. The input location is still inside the triangle. Its output just happens to sit below the reference plane, z equals zero.

4a.text: Here's the sneaky part. If you sketch eight minus four x squared as a familiar parabola, it is very easy to mentally put it on the same axes as the triangle.

4b.text: And on that picture, the parabola seems to cut through the triangle, and then leave it. As if it were fencing off part of the region.

4c.text: But those two pictures use their vertical axes for different quantities. In the triangle's picture, the vertical axis is y. In the parabola's picture, the vertical axis is z.

4d.text: So swing the parabola up, out of the page. Now it stands over the x axis, as a height profile.

4e.text: And since the formula has no y in it, that same profile gets copied straight back along the y direction, wherever the triangle allows.

4f.text: The surface keeps falling, all the way down to negative ninety-two at x equals five. So let's squash the vertical scale to see the whole thing.

4g.text: The parabola never fences in the region. The triangle alone decides where we integrate. The parabola only decides how high.

5a.text: Now slide x across. On the floor, the bright strip shows the allowed inputs at that x: y runs from x up to five.

5b.text: The curtain attached to the strip shows the height assigned to them. Eight minus four x squared, the same all the way along.

5c.text: As x grows, the strip gets shorter, and the height drops below zero. The inputs never leave the triangle.

6a.text: So are we ignoring y? No. A formula with no y in it means that changing y, while keeping x fixed, does not change the output.

6b.text: For example, f of two, two, f of two, three, and f of two, five, are all negative eight. Three different input locations, one height. The surface runs level along the y direction.

6c.text: And y still matters to the average, because the triangle gives different amounts of area at different x values.

6d.text: For a fixed x, y runs from x to five. So the strip of allowed y values has length five minus x.

6e.text: Integrating in y makes that explicit. The integral from x to five, of eight minus four x squared, d y, equals eight minus four x squared, times five minus x. Height, times length. That's the area of the curtain.

6f.text: So the average becomes two over twenty-five, times the integral from zero to five, of height, times length of the strip, d x.

6g.text: The function supplies the height. The region supplies how much area receives that height.

7a.text: So what area goes in the denominator? For the average value of f over D, the definition is: one over the area of D, times the double integral of f over D.

7b.text: Imagine dividing the input triangle into tiny, equal-area tiles, taking the function's value at each tile, and averaging those numbers.

7c.text: Make the tiles smaller, and that simple average settles down. That is all this formula does.

7d.text: So the denominator is the area of the specified triangle, in the x y plane. Not the area of the curved surface. And not the area of a cross section.

8a.text: Here's an electronics version. Imagine D is a triangular circuit board, and f of x, y is the voltage measured at each location.

8b.text: A reading of negative eight volts does not remove that location from the board. It contributes a negative number to the average voltage. The height picture works the same way.

8c.text: That also answers the worry about integrating over nothing. Negative function values are still values.

8d.text: When x is bigger than the square root of two, the height goes negative, and those contributions stay in the average. Stopping there would throw away part of the specified region.

9a.text: If you do evaluate it, this particular average comes out to negative twenty-six thirds, about negative eight point six seven.

9b.text: Picture every column leveling out to one common height. That flat slab is the average. And a negative average is perfectly valid.

9c.text: So, the takeaway. Region: right. Function: right. Order of integration: fine. The single fix is the number out front. One over the triangle's area: two over twenty-five.
